```{r download-raw-datasets, include=FALSE}
base_url <- "https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2021/DataFiles/"

for (f in files) {
  dest <- file.path("data/raw", f)
  if (!file.exists(dest)) {

  }
}

list.files("data/raw")
```

```{r load-raw-datasets, include=FALSE}
tibble(
  file   = c("DEMO_L", "ALB_CR_L", "BIOPRO_L", "GHB_L", "BMX_L",

  n_rows = c(nrow(demo), nrow(alb), nrow(bio), nrow(ghb), nrow(bmx),

)
```

# Abstract

**Background.** Elevated albuminuria is an early marker of kidney damage and cardiovascular risk. Its prevalence and correlates among adults who already have metabolic risk factors but still have preserved kidney filtration are less well described in recent U.S. population data.

**Methods.** We used the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) August 2021–August 2023 cycle. Adults aged ≥20 years with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m² (CKD-EPI 2021) and at least one of diabetes, hypertension or obesity were included. Elevated albuminuria was defined as a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio ≥30 mg/g. Survey-weighted logistic regression examined associations of age, sex, race/ethnicity, glycated haemoglobin, systolic blood pressure, body-mass index and smoking status with elevated albuminuria. Analyses used the phlebotomy weight and the NHANES complex design.

**Results.** Of 3,370 eligible participants, 3,270 (401 events) had complete data on the modelled covariates. The survey-weighted prevalence of elevated albuminuria was 10.9% (95% CI 10.0–12.0%). After mutual adjustment, higher age (odds ratio 1.33 per 10 years, 95% CI 1.15–1.55), higher HbA1c (1.52 per 1%, 1.33–1.73) and higher systolic blood pressure (1.25 per 10 mmHg, 1.03–1.52) were associated with elevated albuminuria. Current smoking showed a borderline association (1.73, 1.00–3.00). Sex, race/ethnicity, body-mass index and former smoking were not significantly associated.

**Conclusions.** In U.S. adults with metabolic risk factors and preserved eGFR, age, glycaemic control, systolic blood pressure and current smoking were the characteristics most clearly associated with elevated albuminuria.

# Introduction
Elevated albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio [ACR] ≥30 mg/g) is a marker of kidney damage and predicts kidney disease progression, cardiovascular events and mortality (1, 2). It can occur before estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) declines, making it relevant to risk assessment in adults with preserved filtration (1, 3).

Diabetes, hypertension and obesity identify a population at increased kidney risk (4, 5). Examining albuminuria within this population can help characterise kidney damage that an eGFR threshold alone would overlook. NHANES August 2021–August 2023 combines questionnaire, examination and laboratory data with a complex sampling design, allowing these associations to be examined in a population-based sample.

> **Clinical question**
>
> Among U.S. adults aged ≥20 years with at least one metabolic risk factor (diabetes, hypertension or obesity) and preserved eGFR (≥60 mL/min/1.73 m²), which clinical and metabolic characteristics are associated with elevated albuminuria (ACR ≥30 mg/g)?

To address this question, we constructed a documented, validated analysis-ready dataset for survey-weighted logistic regression, linking source measurements and questionnaire responses with explicit phenotype definitions.

# Methods

## Study design and population
This cross-sectional study used the NHANES August 2021–August 2023 cycle, a multistage probability sample of the civilian non-institutionalised U.S. population. The unit of observation is the individual participant (one row per SEQN).

Eligible participants were adults aged ≥20 years with measured urine ACR and serum creatinine, eGFR ≥60 mL/min/1.73 m², and at least one confirmed metabolic risk factor (diabetes, hypertension or obesity). Pregnant participants were excluded. Phenotype definitions are given in Section 3.3, and the sequential participant flow is described under *Eligibility criteria and creation of the analysis-ready dataset*.

The age threshold was selected for consistency with previous NHANES studies of kidney disease (USRDS; Wang et al., 2020). ACR and serum creatinine were both required because they define the outcome and the eGFR criterion, respectively. The eGFR restriction allowed examination of albuminuria among adults with preserved filtration. Pregnancy alters glomerular filtration and albumin excretion, which affects how both eGFR and ACR are interpreted; only confirmed pregnancy was excluded, and participants with missing or unascertainable status were retained. Participants with indeterminate metabolic-risk status were not eligible, because eligibility required a confirmed risk factor. No further exclusions were applied; participants with missing regression covariates remained in the analysis-ready dataset (see *Missing data*).



## Source-data assessment
Public-use NHANES August 2021–August 2023 component files were obtained from the CDC repository and imported using haven::read_xpt(). Nine components supplied the measurements, questionnaire responses and survey-design variables required for the study. File dimensions and purposes are summarised below.
```{r source-files-structure, echo=FALSE}
source_components <- list(
  DEMO_L = demo,
  ALB_CR_L = alb,
  BIOPRO_L = bio,
  GHB_L = ghb,
  BMX_L = bmx,
  BPXO_L = bpxo,
  DIQ_L = diq,
  BPQ_L = bpq,
  SMQ_L = smq
)

source_roles <- c(
  "Demographics, pregnancy and survey design",
  "Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio",
  "Serum creatinine and phlebotomy weight",
  "HbA1c",
  "Body mass index",
  "Systolic and diastolic BP readings",
  "Diabetes diagnosis and medication use",
  "Hypertension diagnosis and medication use",
  "Lifetime and current smoking"
)

# File overview: all records as supplied
source_overview <- tibble::tibble(
  Component = names(source_components),
  Purpose = source_roles,
  Records = vapply(source_components, nrow, integer(1)),
  Columns = vapply(source_components, ncol, integer(1))
)

# Identifier and linkage checks: retained for reporting in prose
source_id_checks <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  lapply(names(source_components), function(component) {
    x <- source_components[[component]]

    tibble::tibble(
      Component = component,
      Missing_ID = sum(is.na(x$SEQN)),
      Duplicate_ID = sum(duplicated(x$SEQN)),
      Unmatched_ID = sum(
        !is.na(x$SEQN) & !(x$SEQN %in% demo$SEQN)
      )
    )
  })
)

stopifnot(
  all(source_id_checks$Missing_ID == 0),
  all(source_id_checks$Duplicate_ID == 0),
  all(source_id_checks$Unmatched_ID == 0)
)

knitr::kable(
  source_overview,
  col.names = c(
    "Component", "Purpose", "Records", "Columns"
  ),
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste(
    "Overview of the NHANES August 2021–August 2023",
    "source component files."
  )
)
```

Participant identifiers (SEQN) were complete and unique within every source file. Every record in the eight non-demographic components matched an identifier in DEMO_L, with no unmatched component records. These checks supported one-to-one linkage by SEQN. Missing counts and percentages were calculated within each full source component, before study eligibility restrictions. These describe missing values among existing component records, rather than participants absent from that component. Refused and don’t-know questionnaire responses were counted separately from missing values (NA).
```{r source-variable-quality, echo=FALSE}
# Summarise missingness within each complete source component
source_missing_row <- function(data, source, variable, label,
                               questionnaire = FALSE) {

  stopifnot(variable %in% names(data))

  x <- data[[variable]]
  total <- nrow(data)

  tibble::tibble(
    Variable = paste0(label, " (", variable, ")"),
    Source = source,
    N = total,
    Missing_n = sum(is.na(x)),
    Missing_pct = 100 * mean(is.na(x)),
    Refused_DK_n = if (questionnaire) {
      as.character(sum(x %in% c(7, 9)))
    } else {
      "—"
    }
  )
}
```

Missingness varied across measurements and questionnaire items. Large proportions of missing medication and smoking responses cannot be interpreted as non-response alone because question eligibility and planned skips also produce missing values. Questionnaire responses were therefore interpreted alongside screening questions during phenotype construction, as described in Section 3.3. Age, sex and race/ethnicity were complete in the demographics file.

```{r source-demographic-checks, include=FALSE}
demographic_missing <- vapply(

)

stopifnot(all(demographic_missing == 0))
```


```{r range-check, echo=FALSE}
source_range_row <- function(data, variable, label, units,
                             digits = 1) {

  stopifnot(variable %in% names(data))

  x <- data[[variable]]
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]

  stopifnot(length(x) > 0, all(is.finite(x)))

  tibble::tibble(
    Variable = paste0(label, " (", variable, ")"),
    Units = units,
    Minimum = formatC(
      min(x), format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ","
    ),
    Median = formatC(
      median(x), format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ","
    ),
    Maximum = formatC(
      max(x), format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ","
    )
  )
}

source_ranges <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  source_range_row(
    alb, "URDACT", "Urine ACR", "mg/g", digits = 2

knitr::kable(

  caption = paste(
    "Distributions of selected continuous source measurements.",
    "Summaries use all non-missing observations in each source component."
  )

```
Continuous measurements were inspected using their minimum, median and maximum values. Extreme observations, including nephrotic-range ACR and systolic blood pressure above 200 mmHg, were considered clinically plausible and retained. No observations were modified or excluded on the basis of these range checks.

## Phenotype definitions and analysis-ready dataset construction
All variables were derived for the full linked dataset of `r format(nrow(demo), big.mark = ",")` participants; summaries in the following subsections describe adults aged ≥20 years, and study eligibility was applied only after all derivations were complete (*Eligibility criteria and creation of the analysis-ready dataset*).

### Data integration and participant linkage

The nine NHANES component files were linked by SEQN using DEMO_L as the reference population. Left joins retained all demographic records while adding selected measurements and questionnaire responses. The combined dataset contained 11,933 records with complete, unique participant identifiers. Post-join checks confirmed that the participant identifiers and record count were unchanged; participants without measurements in a component were retained, with the corresponding values recorded as missing (NA).


```{r merge-nhanes-component, include=FALSE}
# Confirm uniqueness of SEQN in each source file before joining
source_files <- list(
  DEMO_L = demo, ALB_CR_L = alb, BIOPRO_L = bio, GHB_L = ghb,
  BMX_L = bmx, BPXO_L = bpxo, DIQ_L = diq, BPQ_L = bpq, SMQ_L = smq
)

uniqueness_check <- bind_rows(lapply(names(source_files), function(nm) {
  x <- source_files[[nm]]
  tibble(
    File = nm,
    Rows = nrow(x),
    Unique_SEQN = n_distinct(x$SEQN),
    Duplicates = sum(duplicated(x$SEQN))
  )
}))

# Merge, retaining only the variables required for subsequent derivation
ard <- demo %>%
  select(SEQN, RIDAGEYR, RIAGENDR, RIDRETH3, RIDEXPRG,
       SDMVSTRA, SDMVPSU, WTINT2YR, WTMEC2YR) %>%
  left_join(alb  %>% select(SEQN, URDACT), by = "SEQN") %>%
  left_join(bio  %>% select(SEQN, LBXSCR, WTPH2YR), by = "SEQN") %>%
  left_join(ghb  %>% select(SEQN, LBXGH), by = "SEQN") %>%
  left_join(bmx  %>% select(SEQN, BMXBMI), by = "SEQN") %>%
  left_join(bpxo %>% select(SEQN,
                            BPXOSY1, BPXOSY2, BPXOSY3,
                            BPXODI1, BPXODI2, BPXODI3), by = "SEQN") %>%
  left_join(diq  %>% select(SEQN, DIQ010, DIQ050, DIQ070), by = "SEQN") %>%
  left_join(bpq  %>% select(SEQN, BPQ020, BPQ030, BPQ150), by = "SEQN") %>%
  left_join(smq  %>% select(SEQN, SMQ020, SMQ040), by = "SEQN")

merge_check <- tibble(
  Measure = c("Rows in demographic file",
              "Rows after joins",
              "Unique SEQN after joins",
              "Duplicate SEQN after joins"),
  Value = c(nrow(demo),
            nrow(ard),
            n_distinct(ard$SEQN),
            sum(duplicated(ard$SEQN)))
)

knitr::kable(uniqueness_check,
             caption = "Participant uniqueness within each source file")
knitr::kable(merge_check,
             caption = "Row count and participant uniqueness after linkage")

stopifnot(
  nrow(ard) == nrow(demo),
  !anyNA(ard$SEQN),
  anyDuplicated(ard$SEQN) == 0L,
  setequal(ard$SEQN, demo$SEQN)
)
```


### Kidney function and albuminuria

eGFR was calculated from serum creatinine (LBXSCR, mg/dL), age and sex using the race-free CKD-EPI 2021 creatinine equation (Inker et al., 2021):

\[
\text{eGFR} = 142 \times \min(\text{Scr}/\kappa, 1)^{\alpha} \times \max(\text{Scr}/\kappa, 1)^{-1.200} \times 0.9938^{\text{Age}} \times 1.012^{\text{[female]}}
\]

where \(\kappa = 0.7\) (female) or \(0.9\) (male), and \(\alpha = -0.241\) (female) or \(-0.302\) (male). eGFR was calculated for adults aged ≥20 years with non-missing creatinine and recorded sex, and set to missing otherwise. ACR (URDACT, mg/g) was retained as a continuous variable, and elevated albuminuria was defined as ACR ≥30 mg/g.

```{r derive-egfr, include=FALSE}
ard <- ard %>%
  mutate(
    # CKD-EPI 2021 creatinine equation (adults only)
    kappa = if_else(RIAGENDR == 2, 0.7, 0.9),
    alpha = if_else(RIAGENDR == 2, -0.241, -0.302),
    female_factor = if_else(RIAGENDR == 2, 1.012, 1),
    egfr = if_else(
      RIDAGEYR >= 20 &
        !is.na(LBXSCR) & LBXSCR > 0 &
        RIAGENDR %in% c(1, 2),
      142 *
        pmin(LBXSCR / kappa, 1)^alpha *
        pmax(LBXSCR / kappa, 1)^(-1.200) *
        0.9938^RIDAGEYR *
        female_factor,
      NA_real_
    ),
    # Elevated albuminuria
    elevated_acr = if_else(!is.na(URDACT), URDACT >= 30, NA)
  )

kidney_check <- ard %>%
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20) %>%
  summarise(
    n_adults          = n(),
    n_with_creatinine = sum(!is.na(LBXSCR)),
    n_with_egfr       = sum(!is.na(egfr)),
    egfr_min          = min(egfr, na.rm = TRUE),
    egfr_median       = median(egfr, na.rm = TRUE),
    egfr_max          = max(egfr, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_egfr_lt_60      = sum(egfr < 60, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_with_acr        = sum(!is.na(URDACT)),
    n_acr_ge_30       = sum(elevated_acr, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_with_both       = sum(!is.na(URDACT) & !is.na(LBXSCR))
  )

knitr::kable(
  kidney_check,
  digits = 1,
  caption = "Kidney function and albuminuria: availability and distribution after derivation"
)
```
Among `r format(kidney_check$n_adults, big.mark = ",")` adults, serum creatinine was available for `r format(kidney_check$n_with_creatinine, big.mark = ",")`, all of whom had eGFR calculated. Median eGFR was `r round(kidney_check$egfr_median, 1)` mL/min/1.73 m² (range `r round(kidney_check$egfr_min, 1)`–`r round(kidney_check$egfr_max, 1)`). Urine ACR was available for `r format(kidney_check$n_with_acr, big.mark = ",")` adults, and both measurements for `r format(kidney_check$n_with_both, big.mark = ",")`.

### Mean blood pressure

Blood pressure was measured with the NHANES oscillometric protocol: after five minutes of seated rest, up to three consecutive readings were taken approximately 60 seconds apart with an automated upper-arm device. Mean systolic and diastolic blood pressure were calculated separately from all available readings, including the first, and were set to missing when no reading was available.
```{r derive-bp-measure, include=FALSE}
ard <- ard %>%
  mutate(
    mean_sbp = rowMeans(
      pick(BPXOSY1, BPXOSY2, BPXOSY3),
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    mean_dbp = rowMeans(
      pick(BPXODI1, BPXODI2, BPXODI3),
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    mean_sbp = if_else(is.nan(mean_sbp), NA_real_, mean_sbp),
    mean_dbp = if_else(is.nan(mean_dbp), NA_real_, mean_dbp)
  )

bp_summary <- ard %>%
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20) %>%
  summarise(
    n_adults    = n(),
    n_with_sbp  = sum(!is.na(mean_sbp)),
    n_with_dbp  = sum(!is.na(mean_dbp)),
    sbp_min     = min(mean_sbp, na.rm = TRUE),
    sbp_median  = median(mean_sbp, na.rm = TRUE),
    sbp_max     = max(mean_sbp, na.rm = TRUE),
    dbp_min     = min(mean_dbp, na.rm = TRUE),
    dbp_median  = median(mean_dbp, na.rm = TRUE),
    dbp_max     = max(mean_dbp, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

knitr::kable(
  bp_summary,
  digits = 1,
  caption = "Availability and distribution of mean blood-pressure measurements among adults"
)
```
```{r bp-reading-counts, include=FALSE}
bp_reading_counts <- ard %>%
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20) %>%
  mutate(
    n_sbp = rowSums(!is.na(pick(BPXOSY1, BPXOSY2, BPXOSY3))),
    n_dbp = rowSums(!is.na(pick(BPXODI1, BPXODI2, BPXODI3)))
  )

# Confirm equal numbers of systolic and diastolic readings
stopifnot(all(bp_reading_counts$n_sbp == bp_reading_counts$n_dbp))

n_bp3 <- sum(bp_reading_counts$n_sbp == 3)
n_bp2 <- sum(bp_reading_counts$n_sbp == 2)
n_bp1 <- sum(bp_reading_counts$n_sbp == 1)

bp_reading_counts %>%
  filter(n_sbp > 0) %>%
  count(Readings = n_sbp, name = "N") %>%
  arrange(desc(Readings)) %>%
  mutate(Readings = c("One", "Two", "Three")[Readings]) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    caption = paste(
      "Number of available systolic and diastolic blood-pressure",
      "readings among adults with a calculated mean"
    )
  )
```
Among `r format(bp_summary$n_adults, big.mark = ",")` adults, mean systolic and diastolic blood pressure could be calculated for `r format(bp_summary$n_with_sbp, big.mark = ",")` (`r round(100 * bp_summary$n_with_sbp / bp_summary$n_adults, 1)`%); `r format(n_bp3, big.mark = ",")` had three readings, `r n_bp2` two and `r n_bp1` one. Median systolic blood pressure was `r round(bp_summary$sbp_median, 1)` mmHg (range `r round(bp_summary$sbp_min, 1)`–`r round(bp_summary$sbp_max, 1)`) and median diastolic blood pressure `r round(bp_summary$dbp_median, 1)` mmHg (range `r round(bp_summary$dbp_min, 1)`–`r round(bp_summary$dbp_max, 1)`). Extreme means were retained as physiologically plausible; excluding them would remove participants with severe hypertension, who are central to the question.

### Diabetes

Diabetes was classified as **present** if any of the following was true:

- self-reported physician diagnosis (DIQ010 = 1), **or**
- HbA1c ≥ 6.5 %, **or**
- current insulin use (DIQ050 = 1), **or**
- current use of diabetes pills (DIQ070 = 1).

Diabetes was classified as **absent** in either of the following situations:

- the participant reported no diagnosis (DIQ010 = 2) **and** HbA1c was measured and below 6.5 %, **or**
- the participant reported borderline diabetes (DIQ010 = 3), HbA1c was measured and below 6.5 %, **and** neither insulin nor diabetes pills were reported.

Insulin use was asked only of participants reporting diagnosed diabetes, and diabetes pill use only of those reporting diagnosed or borderline diabetes or prediabetes; the resulting structural missingness was treated as non-informative. In all other cases diabetes status was left **indeterminate**.

```{r dm-derive}
ard <- ard %>%
  mutate(
    diabetes = case_when(
  # Present
  DIQ010 == 1 | LBXGH >= 6.5 | DIQ050 == 1 | DIQ070 == 1 ~ 1,

  # Absent: clear negative self-report + measured HbA1c < 6.5
  DIQ010 == 2 & !is.na(LBXGH) & LBXGH < 6.5 ~ 0,

  # Absent: borderline self-report, no diabetes medication, measured HbA1c < 6.5
  DIQ010 == 3 & !is.na(LBXGH) & LBXGH < 6.5 &
    (is.na(DIQ050) | DIQ050 != 1) &
    (is.na(DIQ070) | DIQ070 != 1) ~ 0,

  # Indeterminate
  TRUE ~ NA_real_
)
  )

```

### Hypertension

Hypertension was classified as **present** if any of the following was true:

- self-reported physician diagnosis (BPQ020 = 1), **or**
- current use of prescribed medication for high blood pressure (BPQ150 = 1), **or**
- mean systolic blood pressure ≥ 130 mmHg, **or**
- mean diastolic blood pressure ≥ 80 mmHg.

Hypertension was classified as **absent** only when both of the following held:

- the participant reported no previous diagnosis (BPQ020 = 2), **and**
- both mean systolic and mean diastolic blood pressure were measured and were below the thresholds above.

When a participant reported no diagnosis, the medication item was not asked; the resulting structural missingness was treated as non-informative. In all other cases hypertension status was left **indeterminate**.
The blood-pressure thresholds follow the 2017 ACC/AHA guideline definition of hypertension (≥130/80 mmHg; Whelton et al., 2018).


```{r htn-derive}

ard <- ard %>%
  mutate(
    hypertension = case_when(
      BPQ020 == 1 |
        BPQ150 == 1 |
        mean_sbp >= 130 |
        mean_dbp >= 80 ~ 1,

      BPQ020 == 2 &
        !is.na(mean_sbp) &
        !is.na(mean_dbp) &
        mean_sbp < 130 &
        mean_dbp < 80 ~ 0,

      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )

```

### Obesity

Obesity was classified as **present** if body mass index (BMI) was ≥ 30 kg/m² (BMXBMI).  

Obesity was classified as **absent** if BMI was measured and was below 30 kg/m².  

Participants without a valid BMI measurement were classified as **indeterminate**. 


```{r obesity-derive}
ard <- ard %>%
  mutate(
    obesity = case_when(
      !is.na(BMXBMI) & BMXBMI >= 30 ~ 1,
      !is.na(BMXBMI) & BMXBMI < 30 ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )


```

### Combined metabolic risk

The three phenotypes (diabetes, hypertension and obesity) were combined into a single indicator variable (`metabolic_risk`). A participant was classified as having metabolic risk if at least one phenotype was present. The indicator was absent only when all three phenotypes were absent, and indeterminate otherwise.


```{r metabolic-risk-derive}
ard <- ard %>%
  mutate(
    metabolic_risk = case_when(
      diabetes == 1 | hypertension == 1 | obesity == 1 ~ 1,
      diabetes == 0 & hypertension == 0 & obesity == 0 ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )
stopifnot(
  all(
    (ard$metabolic_risk == 1) ==
      (ard$diabetes == 1 | ard$hypertension == 1 | ard$obesity == 1),
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
)
```
```{r phenotype-table}
phenotype_table <- ard %>%
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20) %>%
  select(Diabetes = diabetes, Hypertension = hypertension,
         Obesity = obesity, `Metabolic risk (any)` = metabolic_risk) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Phenotype", values_to = "status") %>%
  mutate(
    Phenotype = factor(Phenotype, levels = c("Diabetes", "Hypertension",
                                             "Obesity", "Metabolic risk (any)")),
    status = case_when(status == 1 ~ "Present",
                       status == 0 ~ "Absent",
                       TRUE        ~ "Indeterminate"),
    status = factor(status, levels = c("Present", "Absent", "Indeterminate"))
  ) %>%
  count(Phenotype, status) %>%
  group_by(Phenotype) %>%
  mutate(cell = sprintf("%s (%.1f)", format(n, big.mark = ","), 100 * n / sum(n))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-n) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = status, values_from = cell)

knitr::kable(phenotype_table,
  col.names = c("Phenotype", "Present, n (%)", "Absent, n (%)", "Indeterminate, n (%)"),
  caption = "Metabolic phenotype classification among adults aged ≥20 years, before kidney-function and albuminuria eligibility criteria")

# For the interpretation sentence: indeterminate status among adults never examined
not_examined_ids <- demo$SEQN[demo$RIDSTATR == 1]
ind_dm <- ard %>% filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20, is.na(diabetes))
n_ind_dm     <- nrow(ind_dm)
n_ind_dm_nox <- sum(ind_dm$SEQN %in% not_examined_ids)
```
Most indeterminate diabetes classifications arose because absence required a measured HbA1c: of the `r format(n_ind_dm, big.mark = ",")` adults with indeterminate status, `r format(n_ind_dm_nox, big.mark = ",")` (`r round(100 * n_ind_dm_nox / n_ind_dm)`%) were not examined and therefore had no HbA1c. The combined indicator had fewer indeterminate cases because one present phenotype, including a self-reported diagnosis, was sufficient.

### Demographic and continuous covariates

Age (years), sex and race/ethnicity were taken from the demographic file and retained in their original NHANES coding. Glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c, %), body mass index (BMI, kg/m²) and derived mean systolic blood pressure (mmHg) were retained as continuous covariates.

### Smoking status

Smoking status was classified from self-reported lifetime and current cigarette use:

- **Never** — smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in lifetime (SMQ020 = 2).  
- **Former** — smoked at least 100 cigarettes (SMQ020 = 1) and now smokes not at all (SMQ040 = 3).  
- **Current** — smoked at least 100 cigarettes (SMQ020 = 1) and now smokes every day or some days (SMQ040 = 1 or 2).  

Participants with insufficient information were left unclassified (missing).


```{r smoking-derive}
ard <- ard %>%
  mutate(
    smoking_status = case_when(
      SMQ020 == 2 ~ "Never",
      SMQ020 == 1 & SMQ040 == 3 ~ "Former",
      SMQ020 == 1 & SMQ040 %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Current",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    smoking_status = factor(
      smoking_status,
      levels = c("Never", "Former", "Current")
    )
  )

smoking_summary <- ard %>%
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20) %>%
  count(smoking_status, name = "N", .drop = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(
    pct = round(100 * N / sum(N), 1)
  )

```
Among 7,809 adults aged 20 years or older, 4,547 (58.2%) were classified as never smokers, 2,050 (26.3%) as former smokers and 1,183 (15.1%) as current smokers. Smoking status could not be determined for 29 participants (0.4%) because the available questionnaire responses were insufficient for classification. 

### Eligibility criteria and creation of the analysis-ready dataset
Eligibility criteria were applied sequentially, and the number of participants remaining and excluded at each step is shown below.

```{r eligibility-flag}
ard <- ard %>%
  mutate(
    eligible_age = !is.na(RIDAGEYR) & RIDAGEYR >= 20,
    eligible_not_pregnant = is.na(RIDEXPRG) | RIDEXPRG != 1,
    eligible_kidney_measurements = !is.na(URDACT) & !is.na(LBXSCR) & !is.na(egfr),
    eligible_egfr = !is.na(egfr) & egfr >= 60,
    eligible_metabolic_risk = !is.na(metabolic_risk) & metabolic_risk == 1,
    eligible_study = eligible_age &
                     eligible_not_pregnant &
                     eligible_kidney_measurements &
                     eligible_egfr &
                     eligible_metabolic_risk
  )

# Cumulative steps
step_preg   <- ard$eligible_age & ard$eligible_not_pregnant
step_kidney <- step_preg & ard$eligible_kidney_measurements
step_egfr   <- step_kidney & ard$eligible_egfr

flow <- tibble(
  Step = c(
    "Demographic file",
    "Adults aged ≥ 20 years",
    "Not pregnant",
    "Valid ACR and serum creatinine",
    "eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m²",
    "≥ 1 metabolic risk factor (final eligible population)"
  ),
  N = c(nrow(demo), sum(ard$eligible_age), sum(step_preg),
        sum(step_kidney), sum(step_egfr), sum(ard$eligible_study))
) %>%
  mutate(Excluded = c(NA, -diff(N)))

stopifnot(
  all(diff(flow$N) <= 0),
  tail(flow$N, 1) == sum(ard$eligible_study),
  !anyNA(ard$eligible_study)
)

options(knitr.kable.NA = "—")
knitr::kable(flow, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
             caption = "Participant selection flow")

# For text: reasons for exclusion at the metabolic-risk step
n_meta_absent <- sum(step_egfr & ard$metabolic_risk %in% 0)
n_meta_indet  <- sum(step_egfr & is.na(ard$metabolic_risk))
```

```{r eligibility-event-summary}
stopifnot(!anyNA(ard$elevated_acr[ard$eligible_study]))
n_eligible <- sum(ard$eligible_study)
n_events   <- sum(ard$elevated_acr[ard$eligible_study])
```

At the final step, `r format(n_meta_absent, big.mark = ",")` participants were excluded because they had no metabolic risk factor and `r n_meta_indet` because their status was indeterminate. Of the `r format(n_eligible, big.mark = ",")` eligible participants, `r n_events` (`r round(100 * n_events / n_eligible, 1)`%) had elevated albuminuria.


### Missing data

Missingness was assessed among eligible participants for the outcome and the seven prespecified regression covariates to define the complete-case analytic sample.

```{r missingness-summary}
eligible <- ard %>% filter(eligible_study)

model_vars <- c("elevated_acr", "RIDAGEYR", "RIAGENDR", "RIDRETH3",
                "LBXGH", "mean_sbp", "BMXBMI", "smoking_status")

n_miss     <- vapply(model_vars, function(v) sum(is.na(eligible[[v]])), integer(1))
n_complete <- sum(complete.cases(eligible[model_vars]))

# Variables reported as complete in the text
stopifnot(all(n_miss[c("elevated_acr", "RIDAGEYR", "RIAGENDR",
                       "RIDRETH3", "LBXGH")] == 0))

miss_txt <- function(v) sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", n_miss[[v]], 100 * n_miss[[v]] / nrow(eligible))
```

Among the `r format(nrow(eligible), big.mark = ",")` eligible participants, the outcome, age, sex, race/ethnicity and HbA1c were complete. Mean systolic blood pressure was missing for `r miss_txt("mean_sbp")`, BMI for `r miss_txt("BMXBMI")` and smoking status for `r miss_txt("smoking_status")`.

Overall, `r format(n_complete, big.mark = ",")` participants    (`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * n_complete / nrow(eligible))`%) had complete data on all model variables. Missingness for every variable in the analysis-ready dataset, including items affected by planned questionnaire skips, is documented in the accompanying codebook.

### Survey design variables

```{r survey-design-check}
stopifnot(
  all(c("WTPH2YR", "SDMVSTRA", "SDMVPSU") %in% names(eligible)),
  !anyNA(eligible$WTPH2YR), all(eligible$WTPH2YR > 0),
  !anyNA(eligible$SDMVSTRA), !anyNA(eligible$SDMVPSU)
)
```

The phlebotomy weight (WTPH2YR), masked variance stratum (SDMVSTRA) and primary sampling unit (SDMVPSU) were retained and were complete, with positive weights, for all eligible participants.

### Analysis-ready dataset

```{r analysis-ready-dataset}
ard_columns <- c(
  "SEQN", "RIDAGEYR", "RIAGENDR", "RIDRETH3",
  "URDACT", "elevated_acr", "LBXSCR", "egfr", "LBXGH",
  "BPXOSY1", "BPXOSY2", "BPXOSY3",
  "BPXODI1", "BPXODI2", "BPXODI3",
  "mean_sbp", "mean_dbp", "BMXBMI",
  "DIQ010", "DIQ050", "DIQ070",
  "BPQ020", "BPQ150",
  "SMQ020", "SMQ040", "smoking_status",
  "diabetes", "hypertension", "obesity", "metabolic_risk",
  "WTPH2YR", "SDMVSTRA", "SDMVPSU"
)

missing_columns <- setdiff(ard_columns, names(ard))
if (length(missing_columns) > 0) {
  stop("Required columns missing from ard: ",
       paste(missing_columns, collapse = ", "))
}

ard_final <- ard %>%
  filter(eligible_study) %>%
  select(all_of(ard_columns))

stopifnot(
  nrow(ard_final) == 3370,
  !anyNA(ard_final$SEQN),
  !anyDuplicated(ard_final$SEQN),
  all(ard_final$RIDAGEYR >= 20),
  all(!is.na(ard_final$URDACT)),
  all(!is.na(ard_final$LBXSCR)),
  all(!is.na(ard_final$egfr) & ard_final$egfr >= 60),
  all(ard_final$metabolic_risk == 1),
  !anyNA(ard_final$elevated_acr),
  all(ard_final$elevated_acr == (ard_final$URDACT >= 30)),
  all(!is.na(ard_final$WTPH2YR) & ard_final$WTPH2YR > 0),
  !anyNA(ard_final$SDMVSTRA),
  !anyNA(ard_final$SDMVPSU)
)

# Used in the text and DT caption
n_ard_rows <- nrow(ard_final)
n_ard_cols <- ncol(ard_final)
```

The analysis-ready dataset was constructed by retaining the `r format(n_ard_rows, big.mark = ",")` participants who met all study eligibility criteria. It contains:

- the participant identifier and demographic characteristics,  
- the primary albuminuria outcome and candidate regression variables,  
- derived clinical and metabolic-risk indicators,  
- the original measurements and questionnaire responses used to construct those indicators, and  
- the NHANES survey design variables.

Intermediate calculation columns and source variables not used in derivation were excluded. The dataset was saved in RDS format (`data/processed/nhanes_albuminuria_ard.rds`).

```{r export-ards}
saveRDS(ard_final, file = "data/processed/nhanes_albuminuria_ard.rds")
```

## Validation

```{r validation-egfr}
# Reload the exported dataset (used by all validation checks)
ard_reloaded <- readRDS("data/processed/nhanes_albuminuria_ard.rds")

# CKD-EPI 2021 creatinine equation (race-free), written independently of the derivation code
ckd_epi_2021 <- function(scr, age, sex) {
  female <- sex == 2
  kappa  <- ifelse(female, 0.7, 0.9)
  alpha  <- ifelse(female, -0.241, -0.302)
  142 * pmin(scr / kappa, 1)^alpha * pmax(scr / kappa, 1)^(-1.200) *
    0.9938^age * ifelse(female, 1.012, 1)
}

# Reference values from the National Kidney Foundation CKD-EPI 2021 calculator
egfr_tests <- tibble(
  scr = c(0.7, 1.2, 0.5, 2.0),
  age = c(50, 60, 40, 70),
  sex = c(2, 1, 2, 1),
  nkf = c(105, 69, 122, 35)
)

check_egfr <- all(round(ckd_epi_2021(egfr_tests$scr, egfr_tests$age, egfr_tests$sex)) == egfr_tests$nkf)

```

```{r validation-rederive}
v <- ard_reloaded

# Helpers: equality treating NA == NA as a match
same <- function(a, b) all((is.na(a) & is.na(b)) | (!is.na(a) & !is.na(b) & a == b))
num  <- function(x) as.numeric(x)
is1  <- function(x) !is.na(x) & x == 1

# Re-derive from the source columns retained in the ARD
re_sbp <- rowMeans(v[c("BPXOSY1", "BPXOSY2", "BPXOSY3")], na.rm = TRUE)
re_sbp[is.nan(re_sbp)] <- NA
re_dbp <- rowMeans(v[c("BPXODI1", "BPXODI2", "BPXODI3")], na.rm = TRUE)
re_dbp[is.nan(re_dbp)] <- NA

re_egfr <- ckd_epi_2021(num(v$LBXSCR), num(v$RIDAGEYR), num(v$RIAGENDR))

re_dm <- ifelse(is1(v$DIQ010) | (!is.na(v$LBXGH) & v$LBXGH >= 6.5) | is1(v$DIQ050) | is1(v$DIQ070), 1,
         ifelse((v$DIQ010 %in% 2 & !is.na(v$LBXGH) & v$LBXGH < 6.5) |
                (v$DIQ010 %in% 3 & !is.na(v$LBXGH) & v$LBXGH < 6.5 & !is1(v$DIQ050) & !is1(v$DIQ070)), 0, NA))

re_htn <- ifelse(is1(v$BPQ020) | is1(v$BPQ150) | (!is.na(re_sbp) & re_sbp >= 130) | (!is.na(re_dbp) & re_dbp >= 80), 1,
          ifelse(v$BPQ020 %in% 2 & !is.na(re_sbp) & !is.na(re_dbp) & re_sbp < 130 & re_dbp < 80, 0, NA))

re_ob <- ifelse(is.na(v$BMXBMI), NA, as.numeric(v$BMXBMI >= 30))

re_mr <- ifelse(re_dm %in% 1 | re_htn %in% 1 | re_ob %in% 1, 1,
         ifelse(re_dm %in% 0 & re_htn %in% 0 & re_ob %in% 0, 0, NA))

re_smk <- ifelse(v$SMQ020 %in% 2, "Never",
          ifelse(v$SMQ020 %in% 1 & v$SMQ040 %in% 3, "Former",
          ifelse(v$SMQ020 %in% 1 & v$SMQ040 %in% c(1, 2), "Current", NA)))

# Compare each re-derived variable with the stored value
rederive_results <- c(
  elevated_acr   = same(v$elevated_acr, v$URDACT >= 30),
  mean_sbp       = isTRUE(all.equal(num(v$mean_sbp), re_sbp)),
  mean_dbp       = isTRUE(all.equal(num(v$mean_dbp), re_dbp)),
  egfr           = isTRUE(all.equal(num(v$egfr), re_egfr)),
  diabetes       = same(num(v$diabetes), re_dm),
  hypertension   = same(num(v$hypertension), re_htn),
  obesity        = same(num(v$obesity), re_ob),
  metabolic_risk = same(num(v$metabolic_risk), re_mr),
  smoking_status = same(as.character(v$smoking_status), re_smk)
)

check_rederive <- all(rederive_results)

```

```{r validation-source}
# Each source file and the ARD columns taken from it
src <- list(
  DEMO_L   = list(demo, c("RIDAGEYR", "RIAGENDR", "RIDRETH3", "SDMVSTRA", "SDMVPSU")),
  ALB_CR_L = list(alb,  "URDACT"),
  BIOPRO_L = list(bio,  c("LBXSCR", "WTPH2YR")),
  GHB_L    = list(ghb,  "LBXGH"),
  BMX_L    = list(bmx,  "BMXBMI"),
  BPXO_L   = list(bpxo, c("BPXOSY1", "BPXOSY2", "BPXOSY3", "BPXODI1", "BPXODI2", "BPXODI3")),
  DIQ_L    = list(diq,  c("DIQ010", "DIQ050", "DIQ070")),
  BPQ_L    = list(bpq,  c("BPQ020", "BPQ150")),
  SMQ_L    = list(smq,  c("SMQ020", "SMQ040"))
)

# Match ARD participants to each source file by SEQN and compare values column by column
source_results <- vapply(src, function(s) {
  idx <- match(v$SEQN, s[[1]]$SEQN)
  all(vapply(s[[2]], function(col) same(num(v[[col]]), num(s[[1]][[col]][idx])), logical(1)))
}, logical(1))

check_source <- all(source_results)

```

```{r validation-survey}
# Reloaded file identical to the dataset that was exported
check_reload <- identical(ard_final, ard_reloaded) && nrow(ard_reloaded) == sum(ard$eligible_study)

# Full survey design: all participants with a positive phlebotomy weight
survey_frame <- ard %>% filter(is.finite(WTPH2YR), WTPH2YR > 0)

# PSUs per stratum in the full design (must be at least two)
psu_full  <- survey_frame %>% distinct(SDMVSTRA, SDMVPSU) %>% count(SDMVSTRA)
check_psu <- all(psu_full$n >= 2)

# PSUs per stratum within the eligible domain (reported, not a pass/fail check)
psu_domain <- survey_frame %>% filter(eligible_study) %>% distinct(SDMVSTRA, SDMVPSU) %>% count(SDMVSTRA)
n_single_psu_domain <- sum(psu_domain$n == 1)

```

```{r validation-summary}
checks <- tibble(
  Check = c(
    "eGFR implementation reproduces NKF CKD-EPI 2021 calculator values",
    "All derived variables re-derived from source columns and matched",
    "Source values identical to original NHANES files",
    "Reloaded file identical to exported dataset",
    "At least two PSUs per stratum in the full survey design"
  ),
  Passed = c(check_egfr, check_rederive, check_source, check_reload, check_psu)
)

if (!all(checks$Passed)) {
  stop("Validation failed: ", paste(checks$Check[!checks$Passed], collapse = "; "))
}

knitr::kable(
  transmute(checks, Check, Result = ifelse(Passed, "PASS", "FAIL")),
  caption = "Validation of the exported analysis-ready dataset"
)
```

Validation was performed in two stages. Before exporting the final ARD file, the dataset was checked for unique participant identifiers, consistency with every eligibility criterion and the outcome definition, and complete survey design variables with positive weights. After export, the reloaded file was checked as shown in the table above: it was identical to the exported dataset; the eGFR derivation code was compared with the National Kidney Foundation CKD-EPI 2021 online calculator for four test cases, and the results were identical (National Kidney Foundation, 2026); every derived variable could be rebuilt from the source columns in the dataset; source values matched the original NHANES files; and each survey stratum was represented by at least two PSUs in both the full survey sample and the eligible study population.

Together, these checks show that the dataset is internally consistent, traceable to its source and ready for the planned analysis. They cannot confirm that NHANES measurements or self-reported answers are accurate.

Variable definitions, derivation rules and missing-value conventions are provided in the accompanying codebook (`metadata/nhanes_albuminuria_ard_codebook.md`; [GitHub](https://github.com/maheration/HDS_M1_NHANES/blob/main/metadata/nhanes_albuminuria_ard_codebook.md)).

## Statistical analysis
Analyses accounted for the NHANES complex, multistage probability sampling design. The two-year phlebotomy weight (WTPH2YR) was used with the masked variance strata (SDMVSTRA) and primary sampling units (SDMVPSU), because the study required blood laboratory measurements. The survey design was declared in the broader sample with finite, positive phlebotomy weights, with primary sampling units nested within strata. The eligible study population was then selected as a survey subpopulation.

Continuous variables were summarised as survey-weighted means and standard deviations, and categorical variables as survey-weighted percentages. Unweighted sample sizes were reported. Descriptive summaries used available observations for each variable. The prevalence of elevated albuminuria was estimated with a logit-transformed 95% confidence interval. Comparisons between participants with and without elevated albuminuria used design-based t-tests for continuous variables and Rao–Scott adjusted Pearson’s χ² tests for categorical variables.

Survey-weighted binary logistic regression was fitted using survey::svyglm() with a quasibinomial family. The prespecified model included age (per 10 years), sex, race/ethnicity, HbA1c (per percentage point), mean systolic blood pressure (per 10 mmHg), BMI (per 5 kg/m²) and smoking status. Reference categories were male, non-Hispanic White and never smoker. Regression was restricted to participants with complete data on all seven predictors, selected within the survey design. Adjusted odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals were obtained by exponentiating model coefficients and their confidence limits. Model checks comprised the number of outcome events per estimated predictor parameter and exploratory tests adding a quadratic term separately for each continuous predictor.

```{r survey-design}
library(survey)

survey_source <- ard


# Retain participants with valid phlebotomy weights
survey_base <- survey_source %>%
  filter(is.finite(WTPH2YR), WTPH2YR > 0)

stopifnot(
  !anyNA(survey_base$SDMVSTRA),
  !anyNA(survey_base$SDMVPSU),
  !anyNA(survey_base$eligible_study)
)

# Declare the design before selecting the study population
design_full <- svydesign(
  ids     = ~SDMVPSU,
  strata  = ~SDMVSTRA,
  weights = ~WTPH2YR,
  data    = survey_base,
  nest    = TRUE
)

# Select eligible participants within the survey design
design <- subset(design_full, eligible_study)

# Confirm the same participants and ordering as the final ARD
stopifnot(
  nrow(design$variables) == 3370,
  sum(design$variables$elevated_acr) == 417,
  identical(
  as.numeric(design$variables$SEQN),
  as.numeric(ard_reloaded$SEQN)
)
)
```


# Results

## Participant characteristics
Participants with elevated albuminuria were older and had higher mean HbA1c and systolic blood pressure than those without elevated albuminuria (Table 1). The weighted prevalence of diabetes was substantially higher in the elevated albuminuria group (49.8% vs 16.9%, *p* < 0.001), as was hypertension prevalence (83.8% vs 75.0%, *p* = 0.030). Race/ethnicity and smoking distributions also differed between groups. There was little difference in sex distribution or mean BMI.

```{r table1}
library(gtsummary)

ard_reloaded$elevated_acr_f <- factor(
  ard_reloaded$elevated_acr,
  levels = c(FALSE, TRUE),
  labels = c("ACR < 30 mg/g", "ACR ≥ 30 mg/g")
)

ard_reloaded$sex_f <- factor(
  ard_reloaded$RIAGENDR,
  levels = c(1, 2),
  labels = c("Male", "Female")
)

ard_reloaded$race_f <- factor(
  ard_reloaded$RIDRETH3,
  levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7),
  labels = c(
    "Mexican American", "Other Hispanic",
    "Non-Hispanic White", "Non-Hispanic Black",
    "Non-Hispanic Asian", "Other/Multi"
  )
)

ard_reloaded$diabetes_f <- factor(
  ard_reloaded$diabetes, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")
)

ard_reloaded$hypertension_f <- factor(
  ard_reloaded$hypertension, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")
)

ard_reloaded$obesity_f <- factor(
  ard_reloaded$obesity, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")
)

design <- update(
  design,
  elevated_acr_f = ard_reloaded$elevated_acr_f,
  sex_f = ard_reloaded$sex_f,
  race_f = ard_reloaded$race_f,
  diabetes_f = ard_reloaded$diabetes_f,
  hypertension_f = ard_reloaded$hypertension_f,
  obesity_f = ard_reloaded$obesity_f
)

tbl_svysummary(
  design,
  by = elevated_acr_f,
  include = c(
    RIDAGEYR, BMXBMI, LBXGH, mean_sbp, egfr,
    sex_f, race_f, smoking_status,
    diabetes_f, hypertension_f, obesity_f
  ),
  label = list(
    RIDAGEYR ~ "Age (years)",
    BMXBMI ~ "BMI (kg/m²)",
    LBXGH ~ "HbA1c (%)",
    mean_sbp ~ "Mean systolic BP (mmHg)",
    egfr ~ "eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²)",

    race_f ~ "Race/ethnicity",
    smoking_status ~ "Smoking status",
    diabetes_f ~ "Diabetes",
    hypertension_f ~ "Hypertension",
    obesity_f ~ "Obesity"
  ),
  statistic = list(
    all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
    all_categorical() ~ "{p}%"
  ),
  digits = list(
    all_continuous() ~ 1,
    all_categorical() ~ 1
  ),
  missing = "no"
) %>%
  add_overall() %>%
  add_p(
    test = list(
      all_continuous() ~ "svy.t.test",
      all_categorical() ~ "svy.chisq.test"

  ) %>%
  modify_header(

  ) %>%
  modify_footnote_header(
    footnote = paste(

    ),

    replace = TRUE

  modify_footnote_header(
    footnote = paste(

  bold_labels() %>%
```

## Prevalence of elevated albuminuria
```{r prevalence}
prev <- svyciprop(~elevated_acr, design, method = "logit", na.rm = TRUE)

prev_table <- data.frame(
  Prevalence = sprintf("%.1f%%", prev * 100),
  CI = sprintf("%.1f%% to %.1f%%", 
               confint(prev)[1] * 100, 
               confint(prev)[2] * 100)
)

names(prev_table) <- c("Prevalence", "95% CI")

knitr::kable(prev_table, 
             caption = "Survey-weighted prevalence of elevated albuminuria (ACR ≥ 30 mg/g)",
             align = "c")
```
The survey-weighted prevalence of elevated albuminuria was 10.9 % (95 % CI 10.0–12.0 %).

## Associations with elevated albuminuria

```{r complete-case, include=FALSE}
# Scaled continuous predictors required by the locked model
design <- update(
  design,
  age_per10 = RIDAGEYR / 10,
  hba1c     = LBXGH,
  sbp_per10 = mean_sbp / 10,
  bmi_per5  = BMXBMI / 5
)

# Restrict the survey design to complete cases on the seven predictors
design_cc <- subset(
  design,
  !is.na(age_per10) & !is.na(sex_f) & !is.na(race_f) &
  !is.na(hba1c) & !is.na(sbp_per10) & !is.na(bmi_per5) &
  !is.na(smoking_status)
)

cc_summary <- tibble(
  Eligible_N      = 3370L,
  Complete_case_N = nrow(design_cc$variables),
  Events          = sum(design_cc$variables$elevated_acr),
  Excluded        = 3370L - nrow(design_cc$variables)
)

knitr::kable(
  cc_summary,
  caption = "Complete-case sample size for the primary logistic regression model"
)
```
Of the 3,370 eligible participants, 3,270 (97 %) had complete data on the seven predictors and were included in the regression; 100 participants (3 %) were excluded, mainly because of missing systolic blood pressure or BMI. The complete-case sample contained 401 events.

```{r primary-model}
# Set reference categories: Male and Non-Hispanic White
design_cc <- update(
  design_cc,
  sex_f  = relevel(sex_f, ref = "Male"),
  race_f = relevel(race_f, ref = "Non-Hispanic White")
)

# Primary survey-weighted logistic regression
model <- svyglm(
  elevated_acr ~ age_per10 + sex_f + race_f + hba1c +
                 sbp_per10 + bmi_per5 + smoking_status,
  design = design_cc,
  family = quasibinomial()
)

# Extract adjusted ORs and 95% CIs
library(broom)
library(scales)

or_table <- tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
    OR      = round(estimate, 2),
    CI_low  = round(conf.low, 2),
    CI_high = round(conf.high, 2),
    p       = pvalue(p.value)
  ) %>%
  select(term, OR, CI_low, CI_high, p)

# Readable labels
or_table <- or_table %>%
  mutate(
    Characteristic = case_when(
      term == "age_per10"                   ~ "Age (per 10 years)",
      term == "sex_fFemale"                 ~ "Female (vs Male)",
      term == "race_fMexican American"      ~ "Mexican American (vs Non-Hispanic White)",
      term == "race_fOther Hispanic"        ~ "Other Hispanic (vs Non-Hispanic White)",
      term == "race_fNon-Hispanic Black"    ~ "Non-Hispanic Black (vs Non-Hispanic White)",
      term == "race_fNon-Hispanic Asian"    ~ "Non-Hispanic Asian (vs Non-Hispanic White)",
      term == "race_fOther/Multi"           ~ "Other/Multi (vs Non-Hispanic White)",
      term == "hba1c"                       ~ "HbA1c (per percentage point)",
      term == "sbp_per10"                   ~ "Systolic BP (per 10 mmHg)",
      term == "bmi_per5"                    ~ "BMI (per 5 kg/m²)",
      term == "smoking_statusFormer"        ~ "Former smoker (vs Never)",
      term == "smoking_statusCurrent"       ~ "Current smoker (vs Never)",
      TRUE ~ term
    )
  ) %>%
  select(Characteristic, OR, CI_low, CI_high, p)

knitr::kable(
  or_table,
  col.names = c("Characteristic", "Adjusted OR", "95% CI lower", "95% CI upper", "p-value"),
  caption = "Adjusted odds ratios for elevated albuminuria from the primary survey-weighted logistic regression model",
  align = "lcccc"
)
```
Older age, higher HbA1c and higher mean systolic blood pressure were associated with elevated albuminuria after adjustment for the other covariates. Adjusted odds ratios were 1.33 per 10-year increase in age (95% CI 1.15–1.55), 1.52 per percentage-point increase in HbA1c (95% CI 1.33–1.73), and 1.25 per 10 mmHg increase in systolic blood pressure (95% CI 1.03–1.52). Current smoking had an estimated adjusted odds ratio of 1.73 compared with never smoking, although the estimate was imprecise (95% CI 1.00–3.00). No statistically significant associations were observed for sex, BMI, former smoking or the individual race/ethnicity contrasts with non-Hispanic White participants.


```{r model-checks, echo=FALSE, results='hide'}
# Events-per-variable
n_events  <- sum(design_cc$variables$elevated_acr)
n_params  <- length(coef(model)) - 1          # exclude intercept
epv       <- n_events / n_params

tibble(
  Events     = n_events,
  Parameters = n_params,
  EPV        = round(epv, 1)
) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Events-per-variable assessment")
```
```{r linearity-check, echo=FALSE, results='hide'}
# Check linearity by testing a quadratic term for each continuous predictor

quad_age <- svyglm(
  elevated_acr ~ age_per10 + I(age_per10^2) + sex_f + race_f +
                 hba1c + sbp_per10 + bmi_per5 + smoking_status,
  design = design_cc, family = quasibinomial()
)

quad_hba1c <- svyglm(
  elevated_acr ~ age_per10 + sex_f + race_f +
                 hba1c + I(hba1c^2) + sbp_per10 + bmi_per5 + smoking_status,
  design = design_cc, family = quasibinomial()
)

quad_sbp <- svyglm(
  elevated_acr ~ age_per10 + sex_f + race_f +
                 hba1c + sbp_per10 + I(sbp_per10^2) + bmi_per5 + smoking_status,
  design = design_cc, family = quasibinomial()
)

quad_bmi <- svyglm(
  elevated_acr ~ age_per10 + sex_f + race_f +
                 hba1c + sbp_per10 + bmi_per5 + I(bmi_per5^2) + smoking_status,
  design = design_cc, family = quasibinomial()
)

# Extract p-value of each quadratic term
quad_p <- tibble(
  Term = c("Age squared", "HbA1c squared", "Systolic BP squared", "BMI squared"),
  p_value = c(
    summary(quad_age)$coefficients["I(age_per10^2)", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    summary(quad_hba1c)$coefficients["I(hba1c^2)", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    summary(quad_sbp)$coefficients["I(sbp_per10^2)", "Pr(>|t|)"],
    summary(quad_bmi)$coefficients["I(bmi_per5^2)", "Pr(>|t|)"]
  )
)

knitr::kable(quad_p, digits = 3,
             caption = "Quadratic term tests for linearity of continuous predictors")
```
There were 33.4 outcome events per estimated predictor parameter. Exploratory quadratic-term tests provided no evidence of quadratic departures from the assumed linear relationships with the log odds (all p > 0.13).


# Discussion
Among adults with metabolic risk factors and preserved eGFR, approximately one in nine had elevated albuminuria. Older age, higher HbA1c and higher systolic blood pressure were associated with elevated albuminuria after adjustment, while the estimate for current smoking was less precise. Alongside these findings, the study produced a documented analysis-ready dataset with explicit phenotype definitions and checks of internal consistency, providing a reproducible basis for examining these associations.

The associations with HbA1c and systolic blood pressure are consistent with an earlier NHANES III analysis, in which both remained independently associated with albuminuria (Bryson et al., 2006). In the Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, Nam et al. (2013) similarly identified associations with systolic blood pressure and HbA1c in both sexes, and with age in men, although their outcome was restricted to moderately increased albuminuria. The direction of our smoking estimate also agrees with Hogan et al. (2007), who found higher odds of albuminuria among current smokers with hypertension in NHANES III; however, our estimate was less precise, and their study used different, sex-specific ACR thresholds. These findings support the relevance of glycaemic status and blood pressure to albuminuria even within our population restricted to metabolic risk and preserved eGFR. Differences in eligibility, outcome definitions and covariate adjustment limit direct comparison of prevalence and effect sizes across studies.

Combining questionnaire responses with examination and laboratory measurements allowed the phenotypes to capture reported or treated disease alongside abnormal measured values. However, these operational definitions remained dependent on the accuracy and completeness of each source. Questionnaire skip patterns required particular judgement: a missing medication response following a negative diagnostic response did not have the same meaning as an unanswered question that should have been asked. Interpreting these pathways explicitly avoided treating all missing responses as equivalent, although the classification rules still involved assumptions. Retaining an indeterminate category preserved uncertainty when evidence was insufficient. Requiring at least one confirmed metabolic risk factor nevertheless meant that some participants with unrecognised or incompletely measured disease could have been excluded.

Retaining eligible participants with missing regression covariates separated cohort construction from model-specific exclusions and preserved the dataset for descriptive and alternative analyses. Complete-case regression subsequently excluded 3% of eligible participants; this small proportion does not itself rule out selection bias. Preserving the broader survey source also supported declaration of the sampling design before selecting the eligible domain. Consequently, independent reproduction of the survey analysis requires the accompanying workflow and broader source data, rather than the eligible-only ARD alone. These decisions improved transparency and analytical flexibility while making the remaining assumptions explicit.

Strengths included standardised NHANES examination and laboratory measurements. Participant-level linkage checks supported record integrity, while retaining source measurements and questionnaire responses alongside derived variables made phenotype construction auditable. The accompanying metadata documented variable definitions, units, derivation rules and missing-value conventions. The exported dataset was re-imported and validated against the specified eligibility criteria, outcome definition and survey-design requirements. These checks supported structural integrity and internal consistency, but could not verify the accuracy of the underlying measurements or self-reported information.

The cross-sectional design precludes establishing temporal order or causality, and a single urine ACR measurement cannot confirm persistent albuminuria. Self-reported diagnoses and single-examination measurements may also misclassify metabolic phenotypes. Age top-coding at 80 years limits differentiation among older participants and may overestimate eGFR among those whose true age exceeds 80 years, potentially affecting eligibility near the filtration threshold. Blood-pressure means based on fewer readings may be less precise. In addition to the missing-data considerations discussed above, restriction to participants with available kidney measurements and confirmed metabolic risk limits generalisability; the findings concern this selected population with preserved eGFR. Residual confounding remains possible because adjustment was limited to the included covariates. Model assessment was also limited: the events-per-parameter calculation does not establish model adequacy, and nonsignificant quadratic-term tests do not exclude other nonlinear relationships or model misspecification.

Sensitivity analyses using alternative phenotype definitions and missing-data approaches could assess the robustness of these findings. Studies with repeated ACR measurements and longitudinal follow-up would help distinguish persistent albuminuria and clarify temporal relationships.
